  2. \displaystyle V_C=\frac{(N_{W,0}\psi)^{1-\sigma_C}}{(1-\sigma_C)\big(1-\beta g^{1-\sigma_C}\big)}, with \partial V_C/\partial g>0 and \partial V_C/\partial\psi>0;

  3. if g_2>g_1 and \psi_2\ge\psi_1, both classes strictly prefer configuration 2, with no welfare weights chosen and no social welfare function written. Corollary A.3 shows that along the family the source varies, the second hypothesis never holds, and replaces this sufficient condition with a criterion that is necessary and sufficient;

  4. g=Bx_W^{\gamma}, where x_W=x_C is the common reproduction index of Lemma A.1 and not x, which denotes capital per worker throughout; so the order in (iii) is ordinally represented by x_W, and by (A.1) that value is c_C;

  5. if g_2=g_1 then N_{W,t,2}=N_{W,t,1} at every date.

Proof. At an interior rest point (x,\nu,z) is constant, so c_W, c_C and z are, so by (A.0) g_W and g_C are constant; stationarity of \nu makes them one factor g, and N_{W,t}=N_{W,0}g^{t}. The worker’s objective is \sum_{t\ge0}\beta^{t}N_{W,t}^{1-\sigma_W}/(1-\sigma_W); successive terms are in the ratio \beta g^{1-\sigma_W}, which properness places in (0,1), and summing the geometric series gives (i). Differentiating, \frac{\partial V_W}{\partial g} =\frac{N_{W,0}^{1-\sigma_W}\,\beta\,g^{-\sigma_W}}{\big(1-\beta g^{1-\sigma_W}\big)^{2}}\;>\;0, \tag{A.10} in which the factor 1-\sigma_W has cancelled. The sign is bought by the curvature normalisation and not by the felicity, which is negative throughout: drop the 1/(1-\sigma_W) and the surviving factor 1-\sigma_W<0 reverses (A.10). For (ii), P is homogeneous of degree one in (K,N_W), so at a rest point it grows at the workers’ factor (Galindo 2026, §2); with P_0=N_{W,0}\psi the same computation returns the display, and \partial V_C/\partial\psi>0 because 1-\sigma_C cancels there too. (iii) follows from (i) and (ii). For (iv), B>0 and \gamma>0 make u\mapsto Bu^{\gamma} a strictly increasing bijection of (0,\infty), Lemma A.1 identifies its argument across the two classes, and (A.1) evaluates that argument at c_C. (v) is the displayed path with g held. Properness is inherited upward: 1-\sigma_j<0 makes g\mapsto\beta g^{1-\sigma_j} strictly decreasing, so raising g never leaves the admissible set. \square

Corollary A.1 (the equalised-index locus carries no welfare content, and the hypothesis that buys it). Two interior rest points sharing a value of c_C lie on one locus of Theorem A.1, share the reproduction index x_W by (A.1), hence share g by (A.0), hence by A.7(v) have identical worker dynasty paths at every date. The elasticity -(1-\theta)/\theta of (A.3) therefore describes a recomposition at constant continuation, and the welfare content of the fiscal split lies entirely in whether it moves x_W. The locus itself is a stationarity relation rather than a set of attainable rest points, so the corollary binds on the pairs of rest points that lie on it and is silent about the rest.

The neutrality is a knife-edge on the worker’s objective. It holds because that objective is a function of the population path alone: private consumption and the public stock enter it only by moving N_W. Along the locus the worker’s consumption is not constant — by (A.3) it moves with elasticity -(1-\theta)/\theta — so a felicity carrying any direct weight \lambda>0 on c_W would rank the two points apart, by exactly \lambda\,\theta^{-1}(1-\theta)\ln(z_2/z_1). Corollary A.1 is therefore a statement about this objective, not a general welfare neutrality, and it fails the moment consumption is valued for itself rather than for the numbers it sustains.

Corollary A.2 (ranking the two dynastic sizes). The capitalist’s dynastic ranking can reverse in finite time. The worker’s cannot. The three cases below are that fact, not a formula with three variants.

Rank the two dynastic sizes directly, N_{C,t}=\nu N_{W,0}g^{t}. In logs the comparison is a line in the date, \ln(\nu_2/\nu_1)+t\ln(g_2/g_1), so the ranking is settled by the growth ordering before it is settled by anything else. If g_2>g_1, configuration 2 dominates configuration 1 in the capitalist’s dynasty at every date when \nu_2>\nu_1, at every date after the first when \nu_2=\nu_1, and otherwise from the date t \;>\; \frac{\ln(\nu_1/\nu_2)}{\ln(g_2/g_1)} \tag{A.11} onward — a bound that is sharp, since below it the ranking is the other way. If g_2=g_1 the line is flat: \nu_2>\nu_1 gives dominance at every date and \nu_2\le\nu_1 at none, and (A.11) has no content there. If g_2<g_1 the line falls, so a larger class ratio buys dominance only up to the date (A.11) names and the ranking reverses after it — the inequality is the reverse of the displayed one, because dividing by \ln(g_2/g_1)<0 turns it round — and without a larger class ratio there is no date of dominance at all.

The growth ordering does the work in all three cases and it is not inherited: A.7(iii) hypothesises g_2>g_1 for its own conclusion and A.7(v) hypothesises g_2=g_1 for its own, so neither is standing here, and the equal-g case is one A.7(v) puts in play rather than an idle corner. Without the ordering the first clause is false outright: at \nu=(1,2) and g=(1.04,1.02) the second configuration leads at every date through t=35 and has lost the lead by t=36, the crossing falling at t\approx35.70. That pair is one the corollary’s own hypotheses permit rather than one solved for here: A.7 fixes the rest-point setting and holds N_{W,0}, \beta and the curvatures common, and it treats the growth ordering and the \psi side — which is where \nu sits — as separate conditions.

The worker’s dynasty needs none of this, and the reason is the substantive half of the corollary. N_{W,t}=N_{W,0}g^{t} from the proof of A.7 gives N_{W,t,2}>N_{W,t,1} at every date after the first whenever g_2>g_1, with equality at t=0 because the initial population is held common; and the ratio (g_2/g_1)^{t} is monotone, so once ahead it stays ahead. That is the whole of the asymmetry: a crossing needs a level to trade against a rate, the class ratio is the only level available, and the worker’s dynasty has no class ratio in it. So the reversal is a difference between the two continuations rather than a fact about arithmetic. Neither A.7(v), which is the equal-g case, nor (A.10), which signs a payoff rather than a population, is what carries it.

Both rankings here are within one class across two configurations, and neither is a ranking of the configurations themselves. The source declines that second ranking, and declines it twice over: it would need a social welfare function over the two dynastic sizes, the paper writes none, and it adds that writing one would not settle the matter either, since the provision is funded by taxing capital and any ranking must price that transfer on both sides. Nothing here supplies one, and along the family the source varies nothing needs to: the passage following Corollary A.3 shows the two classes’ own rankings agree exactly on (A.14) and conflict exactly off it, so a ranking without weights exists on one side of that boundary and no ranking at all exists on the other. A.7(iii) reaches a joint ordering only where those objectives already agree, which is unanimity rather than aggregation, and Corollary A.1 has already said that the equalised-index locus carries no welfare content at all.

Corollary A.3 (the residue is signed, and the ranking is a closed-form dichotomy). Move the rest point along the family the source varies, \phi at fixed (\tau,i). Then

  1. \psi depends on g only through capital per worker. Aggregate capitalist consumption per worker is c_C\nu = (1-i)(1-\tau)\alpha A x^{\alpha}, in which c_C does not separately appear, so by (A.9) \frac{d\ln\psi}{d\ln g} \;=\; \big[\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha)\big]\,\frac{d\ln x}{d\ln g}; \tag{A.12}

  2. the source’s x(g)=\big[i(1-\tau)\alpha A/(g-1+\delta)\big]^{1/(1-\alpha)} gives d\ln x/d\ln g=-g/\big[(1-\alpha)(g-1+\delta)\big], negative under interiority, so \frac{d\ln\psi}{d\ln g} \;=\;-\,\frac{\big[\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha)\big]\,g}{(1-\alpha)(g-1+\delta)}\;<\;0 \tag{A.13} for every \alpha\in(0,1), \omega\in[0,1) and g>1-\delta. The second hypothesis of A.7(iii) therefore never holds along this family;

  3. with \tilde\beta=\beta g^{1-\sigma_C}, the capitalist’s payoff rises with g if and only if \frac{\tilde\beta}{1-\tilde\beta}\;>\;\frac{\big[\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha)\big]\,g}{(1-\alpha)(g-1+\delta)}. \tag{A.14} The worker’s rises unconditionally, by A.7(i). Both signs of (A.14) occur in the admissible parameter region.

That is weaker than it may read. A.7 hypothesises its rest points rather than constructing them, and g is not a free parameter: it solves the stationary system, so a tuple (\alpha,\omega,\beta,\sigma_C,\delta,g) satisfying or violating (A.14) need not be one that any admissible instrument choice induces. What (A.14) establishes here is the criterion; what the witnesses establish is that the criterion is not one-sided as an inequality in its own arguments. Exhibiting both regimes at rest points the constant-share system actually reaches requires solving that system — done below, for an explicit witness pair, not for every calibration.

Proof. (i) By (A.0'), C_C=(1-i)(1-\tau)\alpha Y and N_C=\nu N_W, so c_C\nu = (1-i)(1-\tau)\alpha Ax^{\alpha}; substituting into (A.9) makes \psi a power of x with exponent (1-\omega)\alpha+\omega=\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha). (ii) Stationarity of x under (A.4) is xg=(1-\delta)x+i(1-\tau)\alpha Ax^{\alpha}, which is the displayed x(g); taking logs, \ln x(g)=\big[\text{const}-\ln(g-1+\delta)\big]/(1-\alpha), and differentiating gives the elasticity. (iii) V_C<0 under \sigma_C>1, and d\ln(-V_C)/d\ln g=(1-\sigma_C)\big[d\ln\psi/d\ln g+\tilde\beta/(1-\tilde\beta)\big]; V_C rises exactly when this is negative, and 1-\sigma_C<0 turns that into the bracket being positive, which is (A.14) after (A.13). \square

  1. Solving (A.14) for the depreciation rate at fixed g gives the threshold explicitly: \delta^{\ast} \;=\; 1-g+\frac{\Lambda\,g\,(1-\tilde\beta)}{(1-\alpha)\tilde\beta}, \qquad \Lambda=\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha), \tag{A.16} with \delta<\delta^{\ast} the conflict regime and \delta>\delta^{\ast} the agreement regime.

Proof of (iv). (A.14) fails when \Lambda g/\big[(1-\alpha)(g-1+\delta)\big]\ge\tilde\beta/(1-\tilde\beta); the two sides are equal at the displayed \delta^{\ast}, and the left side is strictly decreasing in \delta on g>1-\delta. \square

(iv') The threshold is an elementary function of the growth factor once the effective discount is eliminated, and the direction it moves is one inequality in the primitives. The growth factor enters (A.16) twice — in the open, and again hidden inside \tilde\beta — which is why the qualification recorded after (A.16) reads as though that boundary could not be traced at all. The second occurrence comes out exactly: \tilde\beta=\beta g^{1-\sigma_C} gives g/\tilde\beta=g^{\sigma_C}/\beta, and what remains is a linear term and a single power. No auxiliary constant is needed to write it, because the combination that would carry one collapses — 1-\alpha+\Lambda=1+\omega(1-\alpha) — so clearing by 1-\alpha>0, (1-\alpha)\,\delta^{\ast}(g)\;=\;(1-\alpha)\;-\;g\bigl[1+\omega(1-\alpha)\bigr]\;+\;\Lambda\,\frac{g^{\sigma_C}}{\beta}, \tag{A.16$'$} (1-\alpha)\,\frac{d\delta^{\ast}}{dg}\;=\;\Lambda\,\sigma_C\,\frac{g^{\sigma_C-1}}{\beta}\;-\;\bigl[1+\omega(1-\alpha)\bigr], \tag{A.16$''$} so the threshold rises with the growth factor exactly when \Lambda\,\sigma_C\,g^{\sigma_C-1}/\beta exceeds 1+\omega(1-\alpha), and falls otherwise. The curvature needs no value beyond the exponent it already carries, which is the economy (A.14''') buys on the weight, obtained here on the other parameter. The direction is itself a threshold in the growth factor, and it too is in closed form: the two sides of (A.16'') are equal at g^{\dagger}\;=\;\Bigl[\frac{\beta\bigl(1+\omega(1-\alpha)\bigr)}{\sigma_C\,\Lambda}\Bigr]^{1/(\sigma_C-1)}, \tag{A.16$'''$} the exponent being defined because curvature exceeds one strictly, and \delta^{\ast} falls in the growth factor below g^{\dagger} and rises above it. So the weight on owned capital does not decide the direction; it moves the point at which the direction changes. At the source’s calibration with no weight on owned capital that point is about 1.45 — above every growth factor the source reports, and below the closure window of A.12, so the threshold falls where that economy sits and rises inside the window where balancing would have to happen. At a weight of nine tenths it drops to about 0.82, below anything a growing economy occupies, and the threshold rises throughout. That is a criterion in the primitives rather than a report of where one economy happens to sit. The threshold is also never vacuous, and the reason is the standing assumption rather than a further one: subtracting the interiority floor leaves \delta^{\ast}(g)-(1-g)\;=\;\frac{\Lambda\,g}{1-\alpha}\Bigl(\frac{g^{\sigma_C-1}}{\beta}-1\Bigr), whose sign is the sign of g^{\sigma_C-1}-\beta and of nothing else — which is exactly \tilde\beta<1. So wherever the profile is proper the threshold sits strictly inside the admissible range of durabilities, and where it is not, it does not.

Proof of (iv'). Substituting \tilde\beta=\beta g^{1-\sigma_C} into (A.16) and collecting the terms linear in g returns (A.16'), the collapse 1-\alpha+\Lambda=1+\omega(1-\alpha) being what removes the auxiliary constant; the only restrictions used are \beta>0 and \alpha<1, and no logarithm appears, so the substitution is valid wherever (A.16) is. Differentiating a linear term and a power gives (A.16''), and its sign is the displayed inequality because 1-\alpha>0. \square

(iv'') Tracing durability through the full correspondence crosses that boundary once, and what delivers it is two cancellations rather than an estimate. Write g(\delta) for the growth factor the stationary system selects at durability \delta, the other instruments held, and set \mathcal{G}(\delta)=\delta-\delta^{\ast}\big(g(\delta)\big), so that the conflict regime is exactly where \mathcal{G} is negative. Then \mathcal{G}'(\delta)\;=\;1\;-\;\frac{d\delta^{\ast}}{dg}\cdot\frac{dg}{d\delta}, and both factors are bounded by the model rather than by a calibration.

The first bound is the source’s own separation. Its closed form for the rest-point growth factor puts every appearance of the growth factor on one side and every share on the other, and durability appears only on the growth side, in a single logarithmic term. So at fixed shares the share side contributes nothing, and dg/d\delta is minus the ratio of that term’s derivative in durability to the whole growth side’s derivative in the growth factor. But that numerator is one of the three strictly positive summands of the denominator, the other two being the pure logarithm and the public-stock term. A part is less than the whole, so |dg/d\delta|<1 — no magnitude estimated, no calibration used, and no attraction hypothesis of the kind (vii) needs, because holding the shares means there is no loop to attract.

The second bound is (A.16'') read one line further. Adding one and clearing, (1-\alpha)\Bigl(\frac{d\delta^{\ast}}{dg}+1\Bigr)\;=\;\Lambda\Bigl(\frac{\sigma_C\,g^{\sigma_C-1}}{\beta}-1\Bigr), because 1+\omega(1-\alpha)-(1-\alpha) collapses to \Lambda exactly. The weight divides out, and the sign is that of \sigma_C g^{\sigma_C-1}-\beta, which properness settles at once: properness is \beta<g^{\sigma_C-1}, and curvature exceeds one strictly, so the quantity is positive. Hence d\delta^{\ast}/dg>-1 everywhere the paper operates.

The two are exhaustive. Where d\delta^{\ast}/dg is non-negative the product is non-positive; where it is negative both factors lie strictly inside the unit interval in absolute value, so the product is below one. Either way \mathcal{G} is strictly increasing and crosses zero at most once. The conflict regime is a lower interval in durability along the full equilibrium correspondence — the statement (vii) reaches for the weight on owned capital, now reached for the parameter that had been left open, and the qualification recorded after (A.16) is discharged rather than merely narrowed.

Proof of (iv''). Proposition 6 of the source writes the rest-point condition as \mathcal{H}(g)=\mathcal{P}, with \mathcal{H} strictly increasing on the interiority interval and \mathcal{P} a function of the shares alone; durability enters \mathcal{H} and not \mathcal{P}. Differentiating at fixed shares gives \mathcal{H}'(g)\,dg+\partial_\delta\mathcal{H}\,d\delta=0, so dg/d\delta=-\partial_\delta\mathcal{H}/\mathcal{H}'(g). Interiority makes both strictly positive, and \partial_\delta\mathcal{H} is exactly one summand of \mathcal{H}'(g), whose remaining two are 1/g and a positive multiple of 1/(g-1+\delta_G); hence 0<\partial_\delta\mathcal{H}<\mathcal{H}'(g) and -1<dg/d\delta<0. The strict inequality needs only one of those two to be positive, and 1/g is positive unconditionally, so the step does not depend on the public-stock term — which is worth saying because that term vanishes at the boundary of the weight on private consumption, a boundary this setting excludes in any case. The displayed identity for d\delta^{\ast}/dg+1 is (A.16'') plus the collapse above, and \Lambda>0 with 1-\alpha>0 leaves the sign of \sigma_C g^{\sigma_C-1}-\beta, positive under properness and \sigma_C>1. The case split is then arithmetic, and \mathcal{G}'>0 in both cases. \square

  1. The weight on owned capital enters (A.14) linearly, so the conflict regime is an upper interval in it and its endpoint is in closed form. Since \tilde\beta=\beta g^{1-\sigma_C} carries no \omega, the difference between the two sides of (A.14) factors: \frac{\tilde\beta}{1-\tilde\beta}-\frac{\Lambda g}{(1-\alpha)(g-1+\delta)} \;=\;\big(\omega^{\ast}-\omega\big)\,\frac{g}{g-1+\delta}, \qquad \omega^{\ast}=\frac{\tilde\beta\,(g-1+\delta)}{(1-\tilde\beta)\,g}-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}, \tag{A.14$'$} and the second factor is strictly positive under interiority. So (A.14) holds if and only if \omega<\omega^{\ast}, fails if and only if \omega>\omega^{\ast}, and at equality the capitalist is indifferent. The classes therefore agree at every admissible weight when \omega^{\ast}\ge1, conflict at every one when \omega^{\ast}\le0, and are separated by a single cut otherwise.

Proof of (v). \Lambda=\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha) is affine in \omega and \tilde\beta does not contain it, so the displayed difference is affine in \omega with slope -g/(g-1+\delta); the root of that affine function is \omega^{\ast}, and the factorisation is the function written about its root. Interiority gives g-1+\delta>0 and g>0, so the second factor’s sign is fixed and the equivalence follows. \square

Two things about (v) come apart. It is the operation (iv) performs on the depreciation rate, carried out on the one parameter in which (A.14) is affine rather than hyperbolic — which is why it returns an equivalence outright rather than a threshold that then has to be argued monotone. And its reach is wider than (iv)’s: \tilde\beta enters (A.14') as a single quantity, so nothing in it needs a value for \sigma_C, and it holds at every curvature the source admits. The cells reported below are a sample of (A.14') rather than the evidence for it. At the source’s calibration and \sigma_C=2, \omega^{\ast} stays inside [0.82,1.78] across the whole band g\in[0.99,1.05] — so every weight below 0.82 agrees at every growth factor in it, which is a region rather than the three cells the next paragraph reports — and the crossing that paragraph locates is the growth factor at which \omega^{\ast} falls through 0.99.

  1. The cut itself moves with the growth factor, and the direction of that movement is in closed form. Both \tilde\beta and the gross-investment margin depend on g, so \omega^{\ast} is not a fixed number as g varies. Write T=\omega^{\ast}+\alpha/(1-\alpha), which is the whole of the first term of (A.14') and is strictly positive under interiority and convergence. Then \frac{d\ln T}{d\ln g} \;=\;\frac{1-\sigma_C}{1-\tilde\beta}\;+\;\frac{1-\delta}{g-1+\delta}, \tag{A.14$''$} and since T>0 this is the sign of d\omega^{\ast}/dg outright. The cut therefore does not rise as the growth factor rises exactly when (\sigma_C-1)\,(g-1+\delta)\;\ge\;(1-\delta)\,(1-\tilde\beta). \tag{A.14$'''$}

Proof of (vi). By (A.14'), T=\tilde\beta(g-1+\delta)/[(1-\tilde\beta)g], and each of \tilde\beta, 1-\tilde\beta, g-1+\delta and g is strictly positive under convergence and interiority, so T>0 and \ln T is defined. Differentiating \ln T=\ln\tilde\beta-\ln(1-\tilde\beta)+\ln(g-1+\delta)-\ln g in \ln g, with d\ln\tilde\beta/d\ln g=1-\sigma_C, gives (1-\sigma_C)\big[1+\tilde\beta/(1-\tilde\beta)\big]+g/(g-1+\delta)-1, which is the display after 1+\tilde\beta/(1-\tilde\beta)=1/(1-\tilde\beta) and g/(g-1+\delta)-1=(1-\delta)/(g-1+\delta). Multiplying the display by (1-\tilde\beta)(g-1+\delta)>0 turns its non-positivity into (A.14'''), and the two are therefore equivalent rather than the second merely sufficient. \square

Three things about (vi) come apart, and the third does the work. It is a comparison of curvature against durability: the capitalist’s curvature pushes the cut down as growth rises, the survival of the private stock pushes it up, and (A.14''') is the exact balance. It needs no value for \sigma_C beyond the one already inside \tilde\beta — with \tilde\beta carried as the single quantity (A.14') already makes of it, (A.14''') is a polynomial inequality in the primitives and the exponent g^{1-\sigma_C} never appears in it, which is the same economy (v) buys on \omega. And at full depreciation of the private stock the second term of (A.14'') vanishes identically, leaving (1-\sigma_C)/(1-\tilde\beta), which is strictly negative because \sigma_C>1 strictly: at \delta=1 the cut is strictly falling in g at every admissible curvature, and (A.14''') has no content there at all.

(A.14') separates the regimes at a given growth factor, while the rest point solves for g and \omega enters that solution. Write g(\omega) for the growth factor the stationary system selects at weight \omega, other instruments held, and F(\omega)=\omega^{\ast}\big(g(\omega)\big)-\omega, so that (A.14) holds exactly where F>0. Then F'=(d\omega^{\ast}/dg)(dg/d\omega)-1. Under (A.14''') the first factor is non-positive, so if the weight does not lower the growth factor the rest point selects, F'\le-1<0: F is strictly decreasing, it crosses zero at most once, and the conflict regime is an upper interval in \omega along the correspondence and not merely at a fixed growth factor. What that leaves is exactly one sign, dg/d\omega, and it is a property of the source’s stationary system rather than of this criterion. The rest of this corollary settles it: first at a fixed growth factor, and then, in (vii), at a selected one.

That sign decomposes further, as far as the source’s own statements carry. Two of them compose exactly. The source puts the rest-point growth factor in closed form as g=\mathcal{H}^{-1}(\mathcal{P}) with \mathcal{H} a strictly increasing bijection and \mathcal{P} strictly increasing in the reinvested share; and it puts the capitalist’s stationary rate in closed form as i^{\ast}=\mathcal{R}/(1+\mathcal{R}), strictly increasing in a rate index the source writes out — called \mathcal{R} here, since this appendix’s R at A.12(vii) is the remainder and the source’s own symbol for the index is a third object again. Composing the two — which is this note’s step, not the source’s — the growth factor is strictly increasing in that rate index, so \operatorname{sign}\frac{dg}{d\omega}\;=\;\operatorname{sign}\frac{d\mathcal{R}}{d\omega} whenever the other two instruments hold still along the profile. In the source’s expression for \mathcal{R} the weight appears explicitly in exactly two places, and they push the same way: a factor 1/(1-\omega), strictly increasing on [0,1), and the elasticity of the capitalist’s composite in his capital, \alpha+\omega(1-\alpha) — which is precisely the \Lambda of this appendix, under the source’s own name for it, and that name is the symbol this appendix reserves at (A.25) for an unrelated replacement share, which is the collision already flagged after (A.15'). Both are strictly positive and strictly increasing in \omega, and the two transition wedges that multiply them — the capital-side one and the public-stock one — carry g, \delta, \delta_G, \alpha and \tilde\beta and are free of \omega altogether. So every channel through which the weight reaches the rate index in the open raises it.

One channel is not in the open, and it runs the other way. The rate index also carries the capitalist’s valuation of the workforce measured against the scale of his own flow payoff, and that scale is a power of the composite, so the weight reaches the index through it as well. The source signs that valuation positive and reads off its two ends: at zero weight it is proportional to (1-\alpha)(1+\alpha J) and as the weight approaches one it tends to (1-\alpha)J, both with the same weight-free positive factor. Those two are ordered, and the source’s own identity orders them — (1-\alpha)J=1-\eta lies in (0,1) exactly under properness, so 1+\alpha J exceeds J by \eta. The hidden channel therefore falls as the weight rises, against the two that climb. Calling it merely unsigned would have understated it.

It is outrun at every weight, and the reason is a cancellation rather than a magnitude. The source does not leave that valuation implicit: it solves for it, and the solution is affine in the weight, since the scalar equation it satisfies has the weight only in (1-\omega) and in \zeta, both affine, over a coefficient built entirely from technology. So the whole bracket the divergent factor multiplies is affine in the weight. That is the fact that decides it. For any affine B, the numerator of the derivative of B(\omega)/(1-\omega) is B'(\omega)(1-\omega)+B(\omega), in which the weight cancels identically, leaving the single constant B(1); and here B(1)\;=\;1+\frac{k\,(1-\alpha)J}{\mathcal{M}}\;>\;1, with k and \mathcal{M} the coefficients of that same solution, positive and free of the weight, and (1-\alpha)J=1-\eta\in(0,1) by the source’s own identity. The rate index is therefore strictly increasing in the weight at every admissible weight, not merely on net — its derivative is J\,B(1)/(1-\omega)^{2}, and the falling channel is outrun uniformly rather than on balance. So dg/d\omega>0, and by the step above the conflict regime is an upper interval in the weight along the correspondence.

One qualification remains after that, and (vii) settles it. All of the above differentiates at a fixed growth factor, while the growth factor is itself selected: it enters the two wedges, the discount factor and the technology coefficient, and the tax share moves along the profile rather than standing still. The source’s own reported profiles already run the way the result predicts, the reinvestment rate rising substantially with the weight while the split stays at its corner; what follows replaces that corroboration with an argument.

  1. The loop closes, and what closes it is the source’s own stability criterion. The source supplies the instrument for exactly this. It shows that the whole share loop — the map carrying a share pair to the rest point it induces, and back to the shares that rest point in turn induces — acts through a single scalar, whose derivative at a fixed point is \mathcal{L}'=\mathcal{P}_g/\mathcal{H}' with \mathcal{H}'>0; and it records that such a fixed point is locally attracting for the loop precisely when |\mathcal{L}'|<1. Its own comparative static in the reproduction elasticity carries two terms in the bracket and needs a further hypothesis on the growth factor to sign their sum. All of that is the source’s; carrying it to the weight on owned capital is this note’s step, and the difference the next paragraph turns on is what the carry buys.

For the weight on owned capital there is only one term, and that is the whole of the difference. The weight enters the share side of the rest-point condition through the reinvested share and through nothing else: the growth side carries no weight at all; the worker’s tax at the corner is a ratio built from the two transition wedges and the capital share, and those wedges carry the growth factor, the two depreciation rates and the discount factor alone; and the worker’s own wedge at that corner is 1-\alpha. Differentiating the rest-point condition in the weight therefore leaves a single product, \frac{dg}{d\omega} \;=\;\frac{1}{\mathcal{H}'(g)\,\big(1-\mathcal{L}'(g)\big)}\;\cdot\; \frac{\gamma\alpha}{(1-\alpha)\,i^{\ast}}\;\cdot\; \frac{\partial i^{\ast}}{\partial\omega}\bigg|_{g}, whose second and third factors are strictly positive — the middle one is the source’s own partial of the share side in the reinvested share, the last is the paragraph above — and whose first has the sign of 1-\mathcal{L}'(g). So local attraction of the loop delivers the sign outright: at any locally attracting rest point of the share loop, the growth factor rises with the weight on owned capital. Together with (A.14''') that completes (vi) — the conflict regime is an upper interval in the weight along the full equilibrium correspondence, and not merely at a fixed growth factor.

Three conditions travel with (vii). It is stated at the corner in the public-investment split with an interior reinvested share, and at a growth factor where the constrained tax is differentiable. The first is not imported: Proposition A.3 above already gives the corner as the unique stationary split under properness and \theta\in(0,1), and states the inequality that delivers it, so the hypothesis is one this note has restated rather than one it has borrowed on trust. Nothing here shows that such a rest point exists or is attracting; the source’s own comparative static is conditional in exactly the same way, and this inherits that and claims no more. And the attraction hypothesis is load-bearing rather than tidying: at a repelling fixed point the same expression reverses sign, so dropping it would not simplify the statement but falsify it.

The weight is the cleaner instrument, and not by accident of the algebra. The reproduction elasticity reaches the growth factor twice — once directly, and once through the reinvested share — and the two can pull against each other, which is why signing its comparative static needs a condition on the growth factor as well as on the loop. The weight reaches it once. The reason is structural and the source states it plainly: the worker’s problem never sees the capitalist’s payoff, so the weight cannot move the worker’s tax except through the growth factor the two classes share. A parameter that lives inside one class’s objective alone moves the equilibrium through a single channel, and its comparative statics are correspondingly clean. That is a fact about the two-class structure rather than about this parameterisation of it, and it is the sharpest thing the conflict result has to say about the model it sits in.

The claim is checkable against a third parameter and survives. Private durability sits in neither objective — it is a law of motion — and it appears on the growth side of the rest-point condition outright, in the same logarithm that carries the gross-investment margin, as well as in the capital wedge that the worker’s tax and the reinvested share are both built from. So it has a direct channel and two indirect ones, which is more than the reproduction elasticity has and strictly more than the weight. The ordering is therefore not a two-point coincidence: the further a parameter sits from a single class’s objective, the more channels it opens, and the more hypotheses signing its comparative static requires. That count of channels is about the growth side of the rest-point condition, and (iv'') shows it is not what decides the comparative static: the qualification on (A.16) is discharged there, and by a route that needs neither the attraction hypothesis (vii) carries nor any bound on the individual channels.

(A.14''') is two-sided at the very calibration (A.16)’s witnesses use, and the two roles must not be run together. At \beta=0.95, \sigma_C=2 and g=1.02 — the capital share does not enter (A.14''') at all, which itself matters, since (A.16)’s threshold depends on it — the condition holds at \delta=0.06 and fails at \delta=0.01. So the same durability margin that decides which regime the classes are in also decides whether that regime’s boundary can be traced monotonically at all; the first is (A.16) and the second is (vi), and they are different questions about the same parameter.

(A.14') holds g fixed, exactly as (A.16) does, and here the qualification is the sharper of the two rather than the milder. The rest point solves for g, and \omega enters that solution through the capitalist’s own reinvestment rule, so moving the weight moves the growth factor as well as the criterion evaluated at it. What (A.14') alone establishes is therefore that at any given growth factor the two regimes are separated by one weight and the conflict regime is the upper piece — not, by itself, that tracing \omega through the full equilibrium correspondence crosses that boundary once. That last step is what (vi) and (vii) supply between them. It rests on one condition of this note’s own, (A.14'''), which is checkable in the primitives, and on the source’s criterion for which rest points its share loop can select; the sign of dg/d\omega, which was the open premise, is settled by (vii).

(A.16) is what carries the attribution, and the witnesses alone would not. At \alpha=0.35, \omega=0, \beta=0.95, \sigma_C=2 and g=1.02 held fixed, \delta^{\ast}=0.0205: at \delta=0.06 the two sides of (A.14) are 13.57 against 6.87 and both classes gain, and at \delta=0.01 they are 13.57 against 18.31 and the capitalist loses. Only the depreciation rate moves between those two, so durability is what separates them. Both were checked against dV_C/dg computed directly from the payoff, and the signs agree.

That comparison holds g fixed, and g is not a primitive: the rest point solves for it, and \delta enters that solution through x(g). So (A.16) locates the boundary at a given growth factor, and it is not by itself the claim that moving \delta through the full equilibrium correspondence traces the threshold. What survives without that qualification is the weaker and still substantive statement that at any given g private durability decides the regime; (iv') and (iv'') then supply the rest, so the boundary is traced along the correspondence and not only at a fixed growth factor.

Where the source’s own numbers fall. The dichotomy would be an empty distinction if one side of it were unreachable, so the source’s reported economy has to be located. At its calibration — \alpha=0.33, \beta=0.96, \sigma_C=2, \delta=0.08 — and at every weight it reports, \omega\in\{0,0.25,0.5\}, the threshold \delta^{\ast} stays below 0.048 across the whole band g\in[0.99,1.05], against a depreciation rate of 0.08. The two classes agree there, and not marginally. Conflict at that calibration needs a capitalist who weights owned capital close to one: at \omega=0.99 the threshold rises past \delta for growth factors above roughly 1.03. So the conflict regime is real but not generic, and what reaches it is not an unusual social wage — it is an unusual capitalist. Both the threshold form and the original inequality were evaluated at every cell of that band and agree at all of them. The band is not standing in for the source’s own point, because the source has two at that calibration — 1.0103 at zero weight on owned capital and 1.0252 at a half — and evaluating (A.14') at each is sharper than the band: at both, the cut \omega^{\ast} lies strictly above one, at about 1.21 and about 1.02. So at the profiles the source actually reports, the conflict regime is not merely non-generic; it is empty, and the two classes agree at every admissible weight.

Both regimes are reached, not merely stateable. The gap named just after (A.14) — that a tuple satisfying or violating the criterion need not be one any admissible instrument choice induces — is closed for an explicit witness pair. Fixing (\tau,i)=(0.5,0.9) and moving \phi within Corollary A.3’s own family at \phi\in\{0.6,0.8\}, at the calibration of Computation 1 (\alpha=0.33,\ \beta=0.96,\ \gamma=0.5,\ \sigma_C=2,\ \delta=0.08,\ \delta_G=0.05,\ \theta=0.6), with A=B=1 — Computation 1 does not fix either, and A=1 matches the source’s own practice elsewhere in Section 8 — each \phi induces a unique interior rest point via the source’s own Proposition 6 — whose stationary equation is strictly increasing in g and carries the interiority interval \big(\max(1-\delta,1-\delta_G),\infty\big) onto \mathbb{R}, so the induced growth factor is unique — located by bisection on the source’s own instrument for this equation (Computation 5) rather than assumed: g_L\approx1.02913 at \phi=0.6 and g_H\approx1.03701 at \phi=0.8, both proper. At \omega=0.95, (A.14) holds at g_L and fails at g_H: the agreement and the conflict regime are each realised by a genuinely induced, admissible rest point, not merely by a free choice of (\alpha,\omega,\beta,\sigma_C,\delta,g). This is existence by witness, not a claim that the conflict regime is generic — the calibration paragraph above already locates it at the high-\omega corner, and that remains the honest description of where it lives.

One corner of (A.14) needs no witness at all, and it ties the result to the note’s existing objects. The dilution term’s denominator is the gross-investment margin g-1+\delta, which is exactly the numerator of the capital wedge J in (A.6). As growth falls towards the point where gross investment vanishes, J goes to zero — the same limit at which Proposition A.3’s remark says full expropriation stops being excluded — while the dilution diverges, so (A.14) fails and the two classes conflict with certainty there. The public-stock wedge \Omega does not vanish at that point and should not: it carries \delta_G rather than \delta. Two objects derived by disjoint routes turning on one factor is a check this derivation could have failed and did not.

This answers a question the source declines. The source states that ranking two configurations would need a social welfare function over the two dynastic sizes, that it writes none, and that writing one would not settle the matter either, since the provision is funded by taxing capital and any ranking must price that transfer on both sides. All of that stands. But along the family it varies, the ranking question does not need such a function at all, because it has an answer without one. The worker’s continuation rises with the growth factor throughout A.7’s setting, by A.7(i) — the point being not that no hypothesis is in force, since properness for both classes is, but that his direction turns on nothing the capitalist’s side turns on. The capitalist’s rises exactly on (A.14), by Corollary A.3(iii), which is a criterion and not a sufficient condition. So where (A.14) holds strictly, the two classes’ own rankings agree; where it fails strictly, they conflict; and at equality the capitalist is indifferent while the worker still gains, which is an improvement one class does not resist rather than a disagreement. The three cases are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and the two strict ones are each inhabited at the source’s own capital share and depreciation rate. Where the rankings agree, one configuration is preferred by both classes judged by their own objectives, and no weights have been chosen. Where they conflict, no ranking exists that does not choose them.

The content of that is a location, and locations are what the source’s declining sentence lacks. The question is not open everywhere and closed nowhere: it is closed on one side of a boundary written in the primitives, and open on the other. What a welfare function would be for is therefore identifiable — it is needed on the conflict cell and nowhere else — and the case a reader might expect, in which the worker loses and the capitalist gains, does not arise at any parameter. That the worker’s direction is fixed independently of the criterion is doing the work here; were it not, the cells would not partition anything and the boundary would carry no information.

The reach is the family and no more. The dichotomy is stated for the split at a fixed reinvestment rate and a fixed tax, which is the family the source itself varies; it says nothing about configurations that differ in their technology, and it must not be read as though it did. Configurations differing in the tax or the reinvestment rate are reached only in the weaker sense (A.15) and (A.15') supply: an identity in the corresponding elasticity, whose own sign the stationary system fixes and this note does not. Nor does it claim that a welfare function would settle the conflict cell — the source declines that too, in the same breath, and nothing here bears on it.

What Proposition A.7 and the dichotomy (A.12)–(A.14) do not reach is the transition. They compare configurations at rest, each from its own rest point; the source locates the whole gap between the growth-maximising split and the worker’s own in the road to one, and nothing here speaks to it. Nor is the family the only one, and freeing the reinvestment rate does not simply undo the dilution. Let \eta=d\ln i/d\ln g along a family that moves i with \tau held — the same letter the source gives to 1-(1-\alpha)J, and a different object — and write \Lambda=\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha) for the combination already governing (A.13). Then \frac{d\ln\psi}{d\ln g} \;=\;\frac{\Lambda-i}{(1-\alpha)(1-i)}\,\eta \;-\;\frac{\Lambda\,g}{(1-\alpha)(g-1+\delta)}, \tag{A.15} whose second term is (A.13) and whose first vanishes identically when i is held. The factor 1-i in that first denominator is strictly positive wherever the display is used: an interior class ratio requires i<1 (Galindo 2026, Theorem 4), so the restriction comes with the hypothesis rather than beside it. Raising the reinvested share lifts capital per worker and cuts capitalist consumption at the same time, and the net effect on \psi is positive only while i<\Lambda. Above that threshold, raising i alongside growth deepens the disagreement instead of closing it. So the conflict of (A.14) is a fact about the family that holds the reinvestment rate, and the reinvestment rate is not a free instrument for escaping it: whether it helps is itself decided by where i stands relative to the capital share adjusted for the weight on owned capital.

Proof of (A.15). By (i), \ln\psi=(1-\omega)\ln\big[(1-i)(1-\tau)\alpha Ax^{\alpha}\big]+\omega\ln x, and by (ii) \ln x=\big[\ln\big(i(1-\tau)\alpha A\big)-\ln(g-1+\delta)\big]/(1-\alpha). Differentiating in \ln g with \tau held gives d\ln x/d\ln g=(\eta-g/(g-1+\delta))/(1-\alpha) and d\ln[(1-i)]/d\ln g=-i\eta/(1-i); collecting the two terms in \eta gives the displayed coefficient, and the remainder is (A.13). \square

The same computation reaches the tax, which is the remaining instrument both families above hold fixed, and there the answer is cleaner than it is for the reinvestment rate. Let \eta_\tau=d\ln(1-\tau)/d\ln g along a family that moves the tax, with \eta keeping its meaning. Releasing both at once, (1-\alpha)\,\frac{d\ln\psi}{d\ln g} \;=\;\frac{\Lambda-i}{1-i}\,\eta \;+\;\eta_\tau \;-\;\frac{\Lambda g}{g-1+\delta}, \tag{A.15$'$} of which (A.15) is the case \eta_\tau=0 and (A.13) the case in which both elasticities vanish. The coefficient on the tax channel is 1/(1-\alpha) before that clearing, and every \omega in it has cancelled. The cancellation is structural rather than arithmetical: at a fixed growth factor the two things \psi is built from are homogeneous of the same degree in the after-tax share. Capital per worker carries (1-\tau)^{1/(1-\alpha)} by the stationary relation of (ii), and aggregate capitalist consumption per worker carries (1-\tau) directly and (1-\tau)^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)} through that same capital, which is again (1-\tau)^{1/(1-\alpha)}. Any weighted geometric mean of two quantities that scale alike scales alike, so the weight cannot appear. The reinvestment rate has no such property: it moves capital per worker at degree 1/(1-\alpha) but capitalist consumption at \alpha/(1-\alpha)-i/(1-i), and two different degrees do not average to one that forgets the weight. That is why its coefficient carries \omega and can change sign, and why the contrast is a finding rather than a restatement.

Two attributions are due. The log-linear decomposition being differentiated is the source’s own, written at its Step 4 for the capitalist’s payoff object; what is this note’s is releasing the tax as a rest-point family elasticity and reading the coefficient off. And the source performs the same cancellation, at that step, on the workforce rather than on the after-tax share — so the technique below is borrowed and only its application is new. A notational warning travels with that: the combination \Lambda=\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha) is the source’s \zeta, while this note’s \zeta at (A.25) is an unrelated replacement share, and the source’s own \Lambda is a third object again. The same holds of \eta: the source writes \eta=1-(1-\alpha)J, which is the sense the identity (1-\alpha)J=1-\eta carries above, while \eta and \eta_\tau from here on are elasticities along a family. And of \psi, where the clash is the sharpest of the four because both objects are functions of the capital stock per worker: this note’s \psi is the capitalist’s payoff object of (A.9), while the source’s is the strong-stable curve z=\psi(x) through the steady state of its autonomous (x,z) block — and the source carries a second \psi besides, a congestion exponent in a counterfactual family, which it discloses itself. The symbols are local to this note throughout, as its numbering is. So of the three instruments the tax is the only one whose weight in his ranking is fixed by the technology outright rather than by how much he values owning capital rather than consuming it — the reinvestment rate’s coefficient changes sign at i=\Lambda, and \Lambda is where \omega lives. It is also of one sign throughout: a family that reaches faster growth by cutting the tax helps him and one that reaches it by raising the tax hurts him, at every weight and every capital share.

Proof of (A.15'). The display in the proof of (A.15), differentiated in \ln g with \tau free, adds d\ln[(1-\tau)]/d\ln g=\eta_\tau to the first logarithm and \eta_\tau/(1-\alpha) to d\ln x/d\ln g. The coefficient on \eta_\tau is therefore (1-\omega)+\big[(1-\omega)\alpha+\omega\big]/(1-\alpha), whose numerator over 1-\alpha is (1-\omega)(1-\alpha)+\alpha+\omega(1-\alpha)=1. Multiplying through by 1-\alpha gives the display, and setting \eta_\tau=0 returns (A.15). \square

On a large class of families \eta_\tau is not a free parameter, and the class is exactly identifiable. Wherever the worker sits at his own stationary tax at the corner in the split, the source fixes that tax in closed form as a ratio built from the two transition wedges and the capital share, and it states that ratio’s arguments outright: the two wedges are functions of the discount factor, the growth factor and the respective depreciation rate, with the capital share entering the second. Writing e_X for the elasticity of X in the growth factor and differentiating that ratio in the growth factor with those arguments held, \eta_\tau \;=\; \tau^{\ast}\Big[\,e_J\;-\;\frac{\theta}{W}\,e_\Omega\Big], \qquad W=\theta+(1-\theta)\Omega, \tag{A.15$''$} so the tax elasticity is a fixed combination of the two wedges’ own elasticities, weighted by the tax itself.

Two restrictions travel with that. The first is which families it covers. What the display computes is the elasticity of the function the source defines, the growth factor moved and the primitives held; it is (A.15')’s \eta_\tau on exactly those families that reach a different growth factor without moving one of the primitives that ratio carries — the capital share, the two depreciation rates, the discount factor. A family that reaches faster growth by making private capital more durable moves the tax through durability as well, and there the two contributions must be added rather than the display used alone. The second is that the two curvatures in play are different and must not be run together: the tax is the worker’s instrument, so e_\Omega and e_J carry his exponent, while the coefficient (A.15') applies to \eta_\tau sits in the capitalist’s index. That is a division of labour, not a conflation.

(A.15'') does not sign itself, and the obstruction is exactly one object. The public wedge’s elasticity has no fixed sign on the admissible region — the gross-public-investment margin dominates it where that margin is small, the discount elasticity dominates where the public stock depreciates fully, and the two pull opposite ways; admissible points of each sign exist. So the qualification below stands for a general family, and what has changed is that the remaining question is a single named elasticity rather than an open choice of family.

The bracket is affine in the worker’s own discount elasticity, so what (A.15'') leaves open is a threshold and not a sign. The growth factor reaches each wedge twice, directly and through the discount factor the wedge carries, so the worker’s curvature does not factor out of either elasticity. But it enters both through that single channel and it enters linearly: each of e_\Omega and e_J is affine in e_{\tilde\beta}=1-\sigma_W, and so, therefore, is their weighted difference. Writing that difference as A+B\,e_{\tilde\beta} — in which the two letters are these coefficients and not the total factor productivity and the reproduction scale they carry at (A.0) and (A.21), a reuse this appendix also makes of \Lambda, \zeta and \eta and flags for the same reason — those coefficients are rational in the capital share, the weight on private consumption, the two depreciation rates, the growth factor and the effective discount, and carry no curvature beyond what that last one already folds in. Which is the qualification that matters here, and it is sharper than the one carried by the earlier thresholds: those hold the growth factor fixed while the rest point selects it, whereas the curvature this threshold is about sits inside \tilde\beta itself. The bracket then vanishes at exactly one curvature, \sigma_W^{\ast}\;=\;1+\frac{A}{B}, \tag{A.15$'''$} taking one sign below it and the other above. Since the admissible curvatures are those exceeding one, the bracket holds a single sign across the whole admissible range exactly when A and B carry opposite signs, and turns over inside that range when they carry the same sign. Both cases arise. At a capital share of one third, a weight of one quarter on private consumption, an effective discount of one half and a growth factor of 1.01, depreciation rates of one twentieth in both stocks place the threshold at 107/12; raising the private rate alone to one quarter carries the threshold out of the admissible range altogether, and there the sign is settled for every worker.

That last number is a threshold in the curvature at a held effective discount, and it must not be read as one in the primitives, because the effective discount is where the curvature lives. Restore it — the effective discount is the discount factor times the growth factor raised to one minus the curvature — and the threshold is the root of an implicit equation rather than a quotient. The quantitative statement does not survive the restoration, and one of the qualitative ones survives only on part of its range: the alternative stated just below is two-way wherever the public stock is the more durable and three-way in general, which the last part of this appendix establishes and exhibits. At the discount factor the source itself uses, with the rest of that first cell held, the turnover falls at a curvature near 1.75 rather than near nine: the effective discount there is about 0.95, not one half. Reaching one half at an ordinary curvature would take a discount factor near one half as well, which is far below anything this model is calibrated with; the effective discount that carries this threshold is the worker’s, since it is his stationary tax being differentiated. So the flip is not the property of an extreme worker that the held-discount number suggests. Where it occurs it occurs just above the logarithmic case, and it occurs at the calibration this note computes on: at Computation 1’s own primitives read at its own growth factor the sign turns at a curvature of about 1.05, which is the logarithmic case in all but name, and at the same primitives read at a slower growth factor it does not turn at all. That is the sharper form of the dichotomy already stated rather than a new one — the threshold either binds once or leaves the sign settled, which is the whole of the alternative where the public stock is the more durable and not elsewhere — and what changes is only where it binds. It binds low. So the disagreement it separates is a live possibility rather than a formal one, which is the opposite of what a threshold near nine would have implied. The two configurations of the previous paragraph behave accordingly: the equal-rate one turns at about 1.75, the durable-capital one does not turn at any discount factor tried and its sign is settled as stated. All of these are computations at named cells, not covers, and where the two depreciation rates differ the location moves with the growth factor as well.

The region does separate on one side, and what separates it is a single comparison between the two depreciation rates. Each coefficient is a ratio whose denominator is strictly positive on the declared domain, so each one’s sign is carried by a polynomial, and the two polynomials are short enough to read. Writing m=g-1+\delta and m_G=g-1+\delta_G for the two gross-investment margins, \operatorname{sign}B=\operatorname{sign}\bigl(m_G-\theta(1-\alpha)\,m\bigr), \operatorname{sign}A=\operatorname{sign}\Bigl(\theta(\delta_G-\delta)\bigl[g^{2}-\tilde\beta(1-\delta)(1-\delta_G)\bigr] +\theta\alpha\tilde\beta(1-\delta_G)\,m^{2} +(1-\theta)(1-\delta)\tilde\beta\,m_G^{2}\Bigr). Interiority puts g above both 1-\delta and 1-\delta_G, and properness puts \tilde\beta below one, so the bracket multiplying the difference of the two rates is strictly positive; the other two terms are non-negative outright. Hence wherever the public stock depreciates at least as fast as private capital, the two coefficients agree in sign — B strictly positive, and A strictly positive except at the single configuration where both stocks depreciate fully. The threshold then exceeds one, and the sign turns over at a curvature the model admits. The excluded configuration is not a blemish but the boundary: at full depreciation of both stocks all three terms vanish together, A is zero, the threshold falls to one, and no admissible curvature turns the sign over at all — which is exactly the corner computed below, reached here as the edge of a region rather than as a separate case.

What that leaves is the other side, and it is not the smaller question it looks like; it is the same question in closed form. For the coefficient on the curvature the answer is already exact and is read straight off the first display rather than argued: it turns negative only where the public margin falls below the private one by more than the weight on private consumption times the labour share, a factor those two primitives fix between them and both of them proper fractions. Durability alone will not do it. What was genuinely open was the other coefficient, and what closes it is that the second display is degree one in the effective discount.

Read as a function of \tilde\beta with the primitives held, the bracket carrying A’s sign is affine, with intercept \theta(\delta_G-\delta)g^{2} and slope \theta(\delta-\delta_G)(1-\delta)(1-\delta_G)+\theta\alpha(1-\delta_G)m^{2}+(1-\theta)(1-\delta)m_G^{2}. Where the public stock is the more durable of the two the intercept is strictly negative, and the slope is strictly positive — its outer two terms are non-negative there and its middle term is strictly positive, since \delta_G<\delta puts \delta_G below one — so the bracket rises strictly in the effective discount and crosses zero exactly once, at \tilde\beta^{\sharp}=\frac{\theta(\delta-\delta_G)\,g^{2}} {\theta(\delta-\delta_G)(1-\delta)(1-\delta_G)+\theta\alpha(1-\delta_G)m^{2}+(1-\theta)(1-\delta)m_G^{2}}\;. So A<0 if and only if \tilde\beta<\tilde\beta^{\sharp}. Durability is necessary; what makes it sufficient is an effective discount below a level those same primitives write down. The two inequalities have become a partition. The gap between the two rates is a factor of that numerator and of the first term of that denominator, and dividing it out says more than the quotient does. Writing \Delta=\delta-\delta_G for the gap, \tilde\beta^{\sharp}=\frac{g^{2}} {(1-\delta)(1-\delta_G)+\dfrac{\theta\alpha(1-\delta_G)m^{2}+(1-\theta)(1-\delta)m_G^{2}}{\theta\Delta}}\;, in which what stands above the gap is exactly the part of the slope that does not carry it. So the threshold falls to zero as the gap closes. A small durability advantage buys almost nothing, and the partition degenerates continuously into the previous paragraph rather than meeting it at a seam. It lies inside the admissible range of effective discounts exactly when that part exceeds \theta\Delta\big[g^{2}-(1-\delta)(1-\delta_G)\big], which is the previous paragraph’s own bracket read at an effective discount of one, now weighing the gap against the part of the slope free of it. The same affinity gives the previous paragraph a second and shorter proof, since a function of degree one on an interval is settled by the values it takes at the two ends and both of those are non-negative wherever the public stock depreciates at least as fast; and it explains why that argument had to be one-sided, because on that side the slope carries no fixed sign at all, and what excludes a crossing there is the pair of endpoint values rather than a direction of travel.

The disagreeing configuration is not merely permitted by the inequality. It is reached, and at the calibration this note has been computing on. The effective discount is not a free primitive: it is the discount factor times the growth factor raised to one minus the curvature, so in a growing economy it falls with the worker’s curvature, from the discount factor itself towards zero, and therefore undercuts any positive threshold at a curvature given in closed form, \sigma_W^{\sharp}=1+\frac{\ln\!\big(\beta/\tilde\beta^{\sharp}\big)}{\ln g}, with the whole admissible range on the disagreeing side when \beta\le\tilde\beta^{\sharp}. A question about whether a region is inhabited has become a threshold in the same object the earlier threshold was in. Computation 1’s own calibration lies on this side — its public stock wears out at a twentieth a period against private capital’s two twenty-fifths — and read at the growth factor this note induces at that calibration — the threshold carries no instrument, only the technology and the growth factor — \tilde\beta^{\sharp} is about 0.94 and the crossing falls at a curvature of about 1.72. That is not an extreme worker. The source fixes its capitalist’s curvature at two and leaves the worker’s free, and a worker as curved as that capitalist is already past the crossing, the two coefficients then carrying opposite signs and the earlier threshold consequently falling below one — which is this note’s second case rather than a new one.

Two qualifications travel with that, and neither is repaired by the above. The reachability argument uses a growing economy: at a growth factor of one the effective discount does not move with the curvature at all, and the question collapses to whether the discount factor itself lies below \tilde\beta^{\sharp}, while in a shrinking one the map runs the other way, so that properness stops being a condition met at every curvature and becomes a ceiling on how cautious the worker may be. The last of those is taken up at the end of this appendix, where the count is settled on that side too. And \sigma_W^{\sharp} is where A changes sign at the induced effective discount, which is not the root of the whole bracket once that discount is restored; at the calibration just used the two lie at about 1.72 and about 1.05, and reading either as the other would give back exactly the distinction the restoration above was made to keep.

Restoring the discount does more than replace a quotient by an implicit equation. It makes the whole curvature ray a single interval, with two ends that can be evaluated. The worker’s curvature reaches the two wedge elasticities only through the effective discount, and the effective discount is his discount factor times the growth factor raised to one minus that curvature. In a growing economy that map is strictly decreasing and carries the admissible curvatures — those above one — onto the effective discounts strictly between zero and the discount factor. Nothing is lost at the far end: every restriction the two wedges impose, the positive public denominator, the positive capital denominator and the two positive gross-investment margins, is loosened rather than tightened as the effective discount falls, and in a growing economy each of them holds at every curvature outright, with nothing assumed at the logarithmic end to secure it. The two ends of the ray are therefore limits and not cells, and both can be written down.

At the logarithmic end the curvature term vanishes with the elasticity carrying it, and the tax elasticity is A read at the discount factor itself, so its sign is the comparison already made above, the discount factor against \tilde\beta^{\sharp}. The other end is the one worth having. Send the curvature up and the effective discount falls to zero; B carries a factor of the effective discount and so dies faster than the curvature grows, and the whole expression tends to

\frac{(1-\theta)\,m_G}{(1-\theta)\,m_G+\alpha\theta\,m}\;\cdot\;\frac{g\,(\delta_G-\delta)}{m\,m_G}, \qquad m=g-1+\delta,\quad m_G=g-1+\delta_G, \tag{A.15$''''$}

the first factor being the limit of the worker’s own stationary tax, which stays strictly inside the unit interval. The bracket it multiplies is signed by the comparison of the two depreciation rates and by nothing else. The capital share and the weight on private consumption survive only in the tax, which is positive, so neither reaches the sign; and the discount factor has left the limit altogether rather than merely its sign, having reached both factors only through an effective discount that has gone to zero. For an indefinitely cautious worker, whether his stationary tax rises or falls as the economy grows faster is settled by which of the two stocks wears out first, and by no other primitive. Where they wear out together the limit is not merely unsigned but zero, and that is the same locus the paragraphs below reach from the other direction: there the capital share leaves the worker’s tax elasticity at every curvature, and in the limit the elasticity leaves with it.

Between the two ends the count of turnovers is not settled by a condition. Write \mathcal{A}(\tilde\beta) for the affine bracket displayed above, the one whose sign is A’s, carrying the intercept \theta(\delta_G-\delta)g^{2} and the slope shown with it. Clear the positive denominator, restore the effective discount, and what carries the sign of the elasticity along the whole ray is \mathcal{S}(\tilde\beta)\;=\;(1-\tilde\beta)\,\mathcal{A}(\tilde\beta)\;+\;\frac{m\,m_G K}{\ln g}\;\tilde\beta\,\ln\frac{\tilde\beta}{\beta}, \tag{A.15$^{\dagger}$} in which K=m_G-\theta(1-\alpha)m is the quantity already shown to carry the sign of the coefficient on the curvature. Since \mathcal{A} is affine, the first term is a quadratic in the effective discount and the second is a constant times \tilde\beta\ln\tilde\beta. Differentiate twice: the quadratic leaves a constant and the logarithm leaves a simple pole, \mathcal{S}''(\tilde\beta)\;=\;-2\,\mathcal{A}'\;+\;\frac{m\,m_G K}{\tilde\beta\,\ln g}, and a constant plus a simple pole is strictly monotone, so it changes sign at most once. The ray carries at most one inflection, at every admissible configuration and with nothing assumed beyond the growing economy that makes the ray an interval at all. That much is algebra and is indifferent to how fast the economy grows; what the growing economy buys is the ray itself, and with it the two ends the count is read from. A function with one inflection has at most three zeros; the two ends fix the parity of that number; and what parity leaves over is settled by which way the curvature runs. No condition on the discount factor is needed anywhere in that, which is why none appears below.

Take the public stock to be the more durable, so that the intercept of \mathcal{A} is negative and its slope positive. If the discount factor does not clear \tilde\beta^{\sharp} both ends lie below zero, and where K is positive the coefficient free of curvature is negative along the whole ray, so the elasticity is negative at every admissible curvature and the sign never turns. If the discount factor does clear \tilde\beta^{\sharp} the two ends disagree, and there the turnover is unique — not under a further condition, but on the whole of that region. K cannot be negative where a turnover exists: a discount factor above \tilde\beta^{\sharp} forces m_G above \theta(1-\alpha)m, so the configuration in which the two coefficients pull against each other and the configuration in which a turnover exists are disjoint. With the slope of \mathcal{A} positive and K positive the carrier is convex and then concave. On the convex stretch the set where it is non-positive is an interval containing the low end, so it crosses upward at most once and is non-negative at the inflection; on the concave stretch it is non-negative at both ends and therefore throughout. One crossing, and the discount factor is asked for nothing beyond the threshold that put the two ends on opposite sides in the first place.

The configuration set aside there is not empty, and it is the one place on this side of the comparison where the sign turns twice. Where K is negative the carrier is concave along the whole ray rather than convex and then concave, and the discount factor then necessarily falls below \tilde\beta^{\sharp}, so both ends lie below zero with room for a rise between them. At a capital share of a tenth, a weight of a half on private consumption, private capital wearing out at four fifths a period against a tenth in the public stock, a discount factor of 0.99 and a growth factor of 1.1, the worker’s stationary tax elasticity is negative at both ends of the ray and positive between curvatures of about 1.85 and about 2.50. Those are not extreme workers, and the band straddles the curvature the source fixes for its capitalist. The concavity supplies the bound and the cell supplies the instance: two crossings there, and never more than two anywhere.

Off that region the alternative is not two-way. Where the public stock is the less durable both ends are positive — the first because the earlier argument puts the curvature-free coefficient positive throughout there, the second because the limit above carries the sign of \delta_G-\delta — so the number of turnovers is even, and by the inflection it is at most two. It is not always zero. At a capital share of one third, a weight of one quarter on private consumption, depreciation of two twenty-fifths in private capital against one tenth in the public stock, the discount factor the source uses and a growth factor of 1.05, the elasticity is positive at the logarithmic worker, negative from a curvature of about 1.45, and positive again beyond about 70. The sign leaves and returns, the first of those crossings at an ordinary curvature rather than an extreme one, so the bound of two is attained and not merely proved. Which side of the comparison the statement is being made on is worth saying, since no configuration computed on here lies on the other one.

Which of the two obtains, where the ends agree, is decided by a parabola rather than cell by cell. A pair of crossings needs the carrier to reach the far side of zero and come back, so it needs a stationary value of the sign opposite to the ends’; and those stationary values are not transcendental, because the equation defining a stationary point is itself a statement about the logarithm. Solve \mathcal{S}'=0 for it and substitute back, and the logarithmic term cancels against the terms it entered with, leaving \mathcal{Q}(\tilde\beta)\;=\;\mathcal{A}'\,\tilde\beta^{2}\;-\;\frac{m\,m_G K}{\ln g}\,\tilde\beta\;+\;\mathcal{A}(0) \tag{A.15$^{\ddagger}$} as the carrier’s value at every stationary point it has — a quadratic built from the affine bracket’s own slope and intercept and the coefficient the carrier already carries. So the count is two exactly when the carrier has a stationary point at which \mathcal{Q} takes the sign opposite to the ends’, and zero otherwise. Since \mathcal{Q} is quadratic, the region on which it takes a given sign is bounded by roots written in the primitives; and whether a stationary point falls inside that region needs no search either. The carrier’s second derivative is strictly monotone, so its first is either monotone or turns exactly once, and in every arrangement has at most two zeros; the sign of \mathcal{S}' at the roots of \mathcal{Q} and at that single turning point, all of them written in the primitives, settles whether either zero falls in the region. What stays out of reach is where the crossings are. The curvatures at which the sign actually turns still solve a transcendental equation, and nothing here puts them in closed form. The count is settled; the location is not.

The same quadratic that decides the count also bounds it, and read the second way it settles every growth factor at once. Divide the carrier by the effective discount. That changes no sign, the ray being strictly positive, and it takes the discount out from in front of the logarithm: \frac{\mathcal{S}(\tilde\beta)}{\tilde\beta} =\frac{\mathcal{A}(0)}{\tilde\beta}-\mathcal{A}'\,\tilde\beta+\mathcal{A}'-\mathcal{A}(0) +\frac{m\,m_G K}{\ln g}\,\ln\frac{\tilde\beta}{\beta}, \qquad \frac{d}{d\tilde\beta}\,\frac{\mathcal{S}(\tilde\beta)}{\tilde\beta} =-\frac{\mathcal{Q}(\tilde\beta)}{\tilde\beta^{2}}\;. \tag{A.15$^{\flat}$} So \mathcal{Q}, reached above by solving for a stationary point and substituting back, is on the other reading what produces those stationary points in the first place: minus the derivative of the reduced carrier. The number of turnovers is then at most one more than the number of sign changes \mathcal{Q} makes along the ray, and \mathcal{Q} is a quadratic whose roots multiply to \mathcal{A}(0)/\mathcal{A}'. So exactly one root is positive, and the reduced carrier turns exactly once, wherever the bracket’s intercept and its slope carry opposite signs. That covers the whole of the region in which the public stock is the more durable — there the intercept is the negative quantity \theta(\delta_G-\delta)g^{2} and the slope is the strictly positive one displayed with it, and the carrier rises before it falls — and it covers configurations on the other side of that comparison too, wherever the slope turns negative, where the intercept is positive instead and the carrier falls before it rises. The direction of the turn goes with the intercept; the count does not. On all of it the count is at most two. That argument uses neither end of the ray, no condition on the discount factor and no sign for K, and it never asks which side of one the growth factor lies on. It therefore subsumes the two paragraphs above rather than adding to them, and it carries to a shrinking economy unchanged.

Read the same display for its extremum rather than for its bound, and the alternative left over at (A.15^{\ddagger}) closes in the primitives. The reduced carrier’s derivative is minus the parabola over the square of the effective discount, so the reduced carrier’s stationary points are the parabola’s own roots — and a quadratic’s roots are written: \tilde\beta^{\pm}=\frac{d\pm D}{2\mathcal{A}'}, \qquad D=\sqrt{d^{2}-4\,\mathcal{A}'\mathcal{A}(0)}, \qquad d=\frac{m\,m_G K}{\ln g}, the affine bracket’s slope standing as the leading coefficient and its intercept as the constant term; where that slope vanishes the parabola is affine instead, with the single root \mathcal{A}(0)/d, and nothing below changes; and where K vanishes with it the logarithm leaves the carrier altogether, which becomes a quadratic in the effective discount and is settled by degree. The value the carrier takes at such a point is written as well, and one identity supplies it. Dividing the carrier by the effective discount and differentiating it are not independent operations, because the two differ by the parabola over that discount: \frac{\mathcal{S}(\tilde\beta)}{\tilde\beta}\;=\;\mathcal{S}'(\tilde\beta)\;+\;\frac{\mathcal{Q}(\tilde\beta)}{\tilde\beta}, \tag{A.15$^{\star}$} an identity in the effective discount rather than a statement at a point. Read where the derivative vanishes it returns (A.15^{\ddagger}), the parabola as the carrier’s value at every stationary point the carrier has. Read where the parabola vanishes the pole goes with it, and what is left is the reduced carrier’s extremal values in the primitives, with the effective discount gone from everything but a single logarithm: \frac{\mathcal{S}(\tilde\beta^{\pm})}{\tilde\beta^{\pm}} \;=\;\mp D+\mathcal{A}'-\mathcal{A}(0) +\frac{m\,m_G K}{\ln g}\,\ln\frac{d\pm D}{2\,\mathcal{A}'\beta}. \tag{A.15$^{\star\star}$}

So where the two ends agree the count is decided by at most two numbers written in the primitives, and the boundary between the counts is an equation rather than a search. A continuous function whose two ends carry one sign reaches the other only at an interior extremum; the interior extrema are the roots above; so the count is two exactly when one of those roots lies inside the ray and (A.15^{\star\star}) carries there the sign opposite to the ends’, and none otherwise — a parabola whose roots both fall outside the ray leaves the carrier monotone across it and the count at none. At most two evaluations settle the matter, a square root and a logarithm each, and the second question the argument at (A.15^{\ddagger}) had to ask — whether a stationary point of the unreduced carrier falls where the parabola takes the opposite sign — does not arise at all, because the stationary points that decide the matter belong to the reduced carrier and are the parabola’s roots. The boundary between the two counts is the vanishing of (A.15^{\star\star}), and it is the only boundary. A root leaving the ray is the other way the test could change its answer, and it never does: as the root approaches either end the carrier’s value there approaches the value at that end, which by hypothesis carries the ends’ own sign, so a configuration counting two keeps its root strictly inside and loses the count only by the value passing through zero. That no single primitive can be solved out of that equation is true, and it is a different statement from the one it is easily taken for: the boundary is an explicit elementary equation in all of them, and deciding which side of it a configuration falls on is arithmetic.

The crossings stay transcendental and stop being unlocated. Between consecutive roots of the parabola the reduced carrier is strictly monotone, its derivative being that parabola’s negative over a positive square, so a sign change is the only one in the bracket it falls in; and the brackets have written endpoints, the two ends of the ray and the roots above. What has no closed form is where a crossing sits inside its bracket. Which bracket holds it, and that it holds one at most, do not depend on finding it.

Which is worth having, because the model reaches growth factors below one, and there the ray runs backwards. At such a configuration the map from caution to effective discount is strictly increasing rather than decreasing: the discount factor is multiplied by the growth factor raised to one minus the curvature, and a base below one turns a falling exponent into a rising power. The ray is therefore (\beta,1), traversed upward, and properness has changed its office. It is no longer a restriction met at every curvature outright but a ceiling on how cautious the worker may be, at \sigma_W^{\max}=1+\frac{\ln\beta}{\ln g}, a finite number. In a contracting economy an indefinitely cautious worker has no well-posed problem, and the far end of the ray is where his discounted total stops converging rather than where his caution runs out. Everything else the two wedges require is met on the whole of that interval, and for the same reason as before read the other way: both denominators are positive because the effective discount stays below one.

The two ends survive the reversal, and one of them becomes the easier of the two. The near end is unchanged — the logarithm vanishes at the discount factor whichever side of one the growth factor lies on, so the carrier there is again (1-\beta)\mathcal{A}(\beta) and its sign is the comparison of the discount factor with \tilde\beta^{\sharp} already made. The far end is new, and it is immediate: at an effective discount of one the quadratic factor vanishes and only the logarithm survives, leaving \mathcal{S}(1)=\frac{m\,m_G K}{\ln g}\,\ln\frac{1}{\beta}, which carries the sign of that coefficient and of nothing else. In a contracting economy the logarithm of the growth factor is negative, so that sign is the opposite of K’s.

Where the public stock is the less durable the direction then turns exactly once, at every admissible configuration, and the parity is the reverse of the growing case. There K is positive outright, so the far end is negative; and the affine bracket is positive across the whole unit interval, which is worth establishing by an identity rather than by inspection, because the identity says more than the sign does. Its value at an effective discount of one is \mathcal{A}(1)=K\,m\,(1-\delta_G)-g\,m_G(\delta-\delta_G), \tag{A.15$^{\natural}$} so where the public stock is the less durable the second term is strictly positive while the first cannot be negative, vanishing only where the public stock depreciates fully — and there the second term carries the whole of it. The bracket, being affine and positive at both ends of that interval, is therefore positive throughout it. The near end is therefore positive and the far end negative, the two disagree, the count is odd, and the bound of the previous paragraph makes it one. In a growing economy that same region carries an even count and two is attained. So the parity of the turnover count is not a property of the region; it is a property of the region and the direction of growth together.

(A.15^{\natural}) does a second job, and it is the one that finds what a search does not.
